title: ORA-01427 Single-Row Subquery Returns More Than One Row: Fix
description: Fix ORA-01427 single-row subquery returns more than one row in Oracle: find the duplicate rows, then use IN, ANY, filters or MERGE, with UPDATE examples.
focusKeyword: ora-01427 single-row subquery returns more than one row

reviewNotes: Examples written from the 19c and 23ai SQL Language Reference; none were run, so every query, error and output (marked expected output) needs a test run, ideally on 19c and 23ai. Please check: (1) FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY inside a correlated scalar subquery (Fix C) works on 19c; (2) the 'rows updated' / 'rows merged' feedback text in SQL*Plus or SQLcl; (3) ORA-30926 message wording differs between releases, so the article quotes the older text only as an example; (4) the 23ai UPDATE ... FROM callout matches the 23ai UPDATE docs (some Oracle blogs credit 26ai, the 23 docs page includes it); (5) the claim that the unique function-based index raises ORA-00001 on a second primary phone. Topic chosen because ORA-01427 is not covered anywhere on the site and autocomplete shows demand for 'ora 01427 how to fix' and 'ora 01427 update'; ranking pages are mostly forum threads without a runnable example or the UPDATE/NULL and NOT IN pitfalls.

data.text: ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row means you used a subquery where Oracle expects exactly one value, and that subquery returned two or more rows. The fix is either to use a multi-row operator such as IN, ANY or ALL, or to change the subquery so it can only ever return one row.

The tricky part is that the same query often works for months and then fails one day. That happens because the error depends on the data, not on the SQL text. In this tutorial you will reproduce the error in the four places it usually appears (WHERE, SELECT list, UPDATE and comparison operators), find the exact rows causing it, and pick the right fix for each case.
What ORA-01427 means

A single-row subquery is a subquery used where one value is expected. Typical places are the right side of =, < or >, a column in the SELECT list, and the SET clause of an UPDATE. A subquery that returns one column from one row and is used as a value, for example in the SELECT list or SET clause, is what Oracle calls a scalar subquery.
The Oracle documentation states the rules clearly. If a scalar subquery returns zero rows, its value is NULL. If it returns more than one row, Oracle raises an error. That error is ORA-01427.

Oracle's own suggested action is: use ANY, ALL, IN or NOT IN to say which values to compare, or reword the query so only one row is retrieved. Which of these is correct depends on what you meant the query to do. That decision is the real work, and the rest of this article walks through it.

data.title: Why the same query works in test and fails in production
data.text: Oracle checks the row count at run time, for each value the subquery is evaluated with. A subquery like (SELECT phone FROM customer_phones WHERE customer_id = 102) is fine until someone adds a second phone for customer 102. Nothing in the SQL changed, but now it fails.
Sample tables for this tutorial
Create three small tables: customers, their phone numbers, and their orders. Customer 102 has two phone numbers, and two customers live in Pune. These two details are what will trigger the error.

data.caption: Sample setup: customers, customer_phones and orders

data.text: Notice that customer 104 has no phone at all, and the phone column in customers is empty for now. Both facts matter in the UPDATE section.
Case 1: = with a subquery in the WHERE clause
This is the most common version. You want all orders from customers in Pune, so you write an equality against a subquery.

data.code:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id = (SELECT customer_id
                        FROM customers
                       WHERE city = 'Pune');
data.caption: Fails: two customers live in Pune

data.code: ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The subquery returns 101 and 103. The = operator can compare customer_id with one value only, so Oracle stops. If you change the city to 'Mumbai', the same query runs fine, because only one customer lives there. This is why the bug often survives testing.
Fix: use IN when you mean "any of these"
Here you really want orders for every Pune customer, so IN is the correct operator, not a workaround.

data.code:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id
                         FROM customers
                        WHERE city = 'Pune')
 ORDER BY order_id;
data.caption: IN accepts any number of rows

data.text: Output (expected output). According to the Oracle docs, IN is equivalent to = ANY, so WHERE customer_id = ANY (SELECT ...) gives the same result. Most people find IN easier to read.
Case 2: a scalar subquery in the SELECT list
Next, you want a report of customers with their phone number. A correlated subquery in the SELECT list looks natural.

data.code:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       (SELECT cp.phone
          FROM customer_phones cp
         WHERE cp.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS phone
  FROM customers c
 ORDER BY c.customer_id;
data.caption: Fails: customer 102 has two phone numbers

data.code: ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The subquery runs once for each customer. For 101, 103 and 104 it returns one row or no rows, which is fine. For 102 it returns two rows, and the whole statement fails. You cannot use IN here, because a column can hold only one value. You have to decide which single value you want.
Fix A: filter to the row you actually want
If the business rule is "show the primary phone", put that rule in the subquery. This is usually the best fix because it states your intent.

data.code:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       (SELECT cp.phone
          FROM customer_phones cp
         WHERE cp.customer_id = c.customer_id
           AND cp.is_primary  = 'Y') AS phone
  FROM customers c
 ORDER BY c.customer_id;
data.caption: Only the primary phone

data.text: Output (expected output). Customer 104 shows NULL because the subquery returned zero rows. That is the documented behaviour, not an error.
Fix B: aggregate when you want all values
If you want every phone number on one line, aggregate inside the subquery. An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, so the error cannot happen.

data.code:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       (SELECT LISTAGG(cp.phone, ', ')
                 WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY cp.phone)
          FROM customer_phones cp
         WHERE cp.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS phones
  FROM customers c
 ORDER BY c.customer_id;
data.caption: All phone numbers in one column

data.text: Output (expected output). LISTAGG over zero rows returns NULL, so customer 104 still shows an empty value.
Fix C: pick one row with a defined order
Sometimes there is no clean filter, and you just need "the most relevant one". In Oracle 12c and later you can use FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY with an ORDER BY that defines what "first" means.

data.code:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       (SELECT cp.phone
          FROM customer_phones cp
         WHERE cp.customer_id = c.customer_id
         ORDER BY cp.is_primary DESC, cp.phone
         FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY) AS phone
  FROM customers c
 ORDER BY c.customer_id;
data.caption: Primary phone first, then the lowest number

data.text: This returns the same result as Fix A for this data. Because 'Y' sorts after 'N', ordering is_primary DESC puts the primary phone first. Without the ORDER BY, Oracle may return any one of the rows, and the answer can change between runs.

data.title: Do not silence the error blindly
data.text: Adding ROWNUM = 1 or MAX() makes the error disappear, but it also hides the question you should be asking: why are there two rows? If the duplicate is a data bug, the arbitrary pick will put wrong values in reports and nobody will notice.
Case 3: ORA-01427 in an UPDATE statement
Copying a value from one table to another with a correlated subquery is where this error hurts most, because it often appears in batch jobs. Here you try to fill customers.phone from customer_phones.

data.code:
UPDATE customers c
   SET c.phone = (SELECT cp.phone
                    FROM customer_phones cp
                   WHERE cp.customer_id = c.customer_id);
data.caption: Fails because of customer 102

data.code: ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: When a statement fails, Oracle rolls back the whole statement, so no customer is updated, not even the ones that had a single phone. Your earlier work in the same transaction is not affected.
Step 1: find the rows causing the error
Before you fix the SQL, look at the data. Group the subquery's table by the correlation column and keep groups with more than one row.

data.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS phone_count
  FROM customer_phones
 GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
data.caption: Which customers have more than one phone?

data.text: Output (expected output). Now you know it is customer 102, and you can decide whether the second row is valid data (a secondary phone) or a duplicate that should be removed. Use this same pattern for any ORA-01427: take the subquery, remove the outer correlation, and group by the column it was correlated on.
Step 2: fix the subquery and protect rows with no match

data.code:
UPDATE customers c
   SET c.phone = (SELECT cp.phone
                    FROM customer_phones cp
                   WHERE cp.customer_id = c.customer_id
                     AND cp.is_primary  = 'Y')
 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
                 FROM customer_phones cp
                WHERE cp.customer_id = c.customer_id
                  AND cp.is_primary  = 'Y');
data.caption: Primary phone only, and only customers that have one

data.text: The WHERE EXISTS clause is easy to forget. Without it, the UPDATE touches all four customers, and customer 104 gets phone set to NULL, because the Oracle docs say a SET subquery that returns no rows assigns a null. On this sample that is harmless, but on a real table it can wipe out values that were already there.
Alternative: MERGE with a clean source
MERGE reads the source once and joins it to the target, which many people find easier to read than two matching subqueries.

data.code:
MERGE INTO customers c
USING (SELECT customer_id, phone
         FROM customer_phones
        WHERE is_primary = 'Y') src
   ON (c.customer_id = src.customer_id)
 WHEN MATCHED THEN
   UPDATE SET c.phone = src.phone;
data.caption: Only matched customers are updated

data.text: MERGE does not raise ORA-01427, but it has its own version of the same problem. If two source rows match one target row, it fails with ORA-30926 (the message text differs between releases, for example "unable to get a stable set of rows in the source tables"). So you still need a source with one row per key. Our Oracle MERGE statement guide covers MERGE in detail.

data.title: Oracle Database 23ai: UPDATE with a FROM clause
data.text: From Oracle Database 23ai you can join directly in an UPDATE: UPDATE customers c SET c.phone = cp.phone FROM customer_phones cp WHERE cp.customer_id = c.customer_id AND cp.is_primary = 'Y'. Rows with no match are not touched. If the join would update the same row twice, the 23ai documentation says it raises ORA-30926.
Case 4: > or < against several rows
The error also appears with range comparisons. Suppose you want orders bigger than customer 101's orders. Customer 101 has two orders (2500 and 450), so the subquery returns two rows.

data.code:
SELECT order_id, amount
  FROM orders
 WHERE amount > (SELECT amount
                   FROM orders
                  WHERE customer_id = 101);
data.caption: Fails: customer 101 has two orders

data.text: Here the right fix depends on the question. "Bigger than all of their orders" and "bigger than at least one of their orders" are different questions, and Oracle gives you ALL and ANY for them.

data.code:
-- Bigger than every order of customer 101 (greater than 2500)
SELECT order_id, amount
  FROM orders
 WHERE amount > ALL (SELECT amount
                       FROM orders
                      WHERE customer_id = 101);

-- Bigger than at least one order of customer 101 (greater than 450)
SELECT order_id, amount
  FROM orders
 WHERE amount > ANY (SELECT amount
                       FROM orders
                      WHERE customer_id = 101)
 ORDER BY order_id;
data.caption: ALL and ANY answer different questions

data.text: You can also write these with aggregates: > (SELECT MAX(amount) ...) and > (SELECT MIN(amount) ...). Be careful with empty subqueries, though. The docs say > ALL returns TRUE when the subquery returns no rows, so every row qualifies. > (SELECT MAX(...)) compares with NULL in that case and returns no rows. Pick the version whose empty-set behaviour matches your requirement.
Common mistakes

items.content: Testing with one parameter value. The query works for Mumbai and fails for Pune. When you see ORA-01427 only in production, run the subquery on its own with the failing value and count the rows.
Using ROWNUM = 1 without ORDER BY. It removes the error but returns an unpredictable row. If you must pick one row, use ORDER BY ... FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY (12c and later) so the choice is defined.

Switching = to NOT IN without thinking about NULLs. For the negative version, people write NOT IN (SELECT ...). The Oracle docs warn that if any value in the list is NULL, no rows are returned. Add WHERE col IS NOT NULL in the subquery or use NOT EXISTS.
Forgetting WHERE EXISTS in a correlated UPDATE. After fixing ORA-01427, rows with no match are silently set to NULL.

Confusing ORA-01427 with ORA-01422. In PL/SQL, SELECT ... INTO that returns several rows raises ORA-01422 (exact fetch returned more than the requested number of rows), which PL/SQL exposes as the TOO_MANY_ROWS exception. ORA-01427 comes from a subquery inside a SQL statement. The diagnosis is similar, but the fixes differ: for ORA-01422 you use a cursor loop or BULK COLLECT.

Fixing the query when the data is wrong. If a customer should only ever have one primary phone, a duplicate primary row is a data problem. Clean it up (see how to delete duplicate rows but keep one) and add a constraint so it cannot come back.

data.text: Best practices to prevent ORA-01427
The most reliable fix is to make the database guarantee that the subquery can only return one row. If the subquery filters on a primary key or a unique key, ORA-01427 is impossible.

For rules like "one primary phone per customer", a unique function-based index enforces the rule while still allowing many non-primary phones. Oracle does not store index entries where all key columns are NULL, so only the primary rows are checked.

data.caption: At most one primary phone per customer

data.text: With this index in place, inserting a second primary phone for customer 102 fails with ORA-00001 (unique constraint violated) at insert time, which is a much better moment to find the problem than in the middle of a nightly UPDATE.

items.content: Index the correlation column (customer_phones.customer_id here). A correlated scalar subquery or EXISTS runs for each outer row, and without an index each run may scan the whole table.
Prefer a join, MERGE or (in 23ai) UPDATE ... FROM for large updates. Write the source as one row per key, using GROUP BY or a filter, and the plan is usually easier to read and tune.

Choose between IN and EXISTS by meaning, not by habit. The optimizer can often transform both into a join, so check the actual plan before assuming one is faster. See how to read an explain plan in Oracle.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
What is ORA-01427 in Oracle?

It is the error Oracle raises when a subquery used in a single-value position (after =, <, >, in the SELECT list or in UPDATE SET) returns more than one row. Oracle cannot decide which value to use, so it stops the statement.
How do I fix ORA-01427 in an UPDATE statement?

Run the subquery on its own with GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to find the keys with several rows. Then add a filter that makes the subquery return one row, or use an aggregate, and add WHERE EXISTS so rows without a match are not set to NULL. MERGE with a de-duplicated source is a good alternative.
Why does my query work for some values and fail for others?

Because the error depends on how many rows the subquery returns for each value, not on the SQL syntax. A value with one matching row works. A value with two matching rows fails. Check the failing value directly.
Can I use ROWNUM = 1 to fix ORA-01427?

It stops the error, but without an ORDER BY you get an arbitrary row, which can change from run to run. Use it only when any row is truly acceptable. Otherwise use a precise filter, an aggregate, or ORDER BY ... FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY.
What is the difference between ORA-01427 and ORA-01422?

ORA-01427 comes from a subquery inside a SQL statement that returns too many rows. ORA-01422 comes from a PL/SQL SELECT INTO (or RETURNING INTO) that returns more than one row, and it maps to the TOO_MANY_ROWS exception.
Summary

items.content: ORA-01427 means a subquery in a single-value position returned two or more rows.
Find the cause with GROUP BY on the correlation column and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
Use IN, ANY or ALL when you really mean a set of values.
In the SELECT list or UPDATE SET, filter to one row, aggregate, or use ORDER BY with FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY.
Add WHERE EXISTS to correlated UPDATEs so unmatched rows are not set to NULL.
Watch NOT IN with NULLs and the empty-subquery behaviour of ALL.
Prevent the error with primary keys, unique constraints or a unique function-based index.

linkedin.post:
Your UPDATE ran fine for months. Today it fails with ORA-01427 and nobody changed the SQL.

The reason: someone added a second row to the lookup table. ORA-01427 depends on the data, not the query text.

What to do:
→ Find the culprit first: GROUP BY the correlated column and keep HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
→ If you mean "any of these values", replace = with IN. It is the correct operator, not a hack
→ In a SELECT list or UPDATE SET, decide which single value you want: filter it, aggregate it, or ORDER BY with FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY
→ After fixing a correlated UPDATE, add WHERE EXISTS. A subquery with no match sets the column to NULL
→ ROWNUM = 1 without ORDER BY hides the bug and returns an arbitrary row

Bonus trap: > ALL on an empty subquery is TRUE, so every row matches.

How do you handle this in batch jobs: fix the query, or add a unique constraint so it cannot happen again?

slides.title: What the error means
points: A subquery sits where Oracle expects one value
It returned two or more rows, so Oracle stops
It depends on data: works for one key, fails for another

slides.title: Find the rows causing it
slides.body: Remove the correlation from the subquery and group by the column it was joined on.
slides.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*)
  FROM customer_phones
 GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

slides.title: Meant a list? Use IN
slides.code:
SELECT order_id, amount
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id IN (
   SELECT customer_id
     FROM customers
    WHERE city = 'Pune');
points: Use > ALL or > ANY for range checks

slides.title: Safer UPDATE: one row per key
slides.body: In a correlated UPDATE, also add WHERE EXISTS, or rows with no match become NULL. MERGE from a one-row-per-key source avoids both problems.
slides.code:
MERGE INTO customers c
USING (SELECT customer_id, phone
  FROM customer_phones
  WHERE is_primary = 'Y') s
ON (c.customer_id = s.customer_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET c.phone = s.phone;

slides.title: Traps to avoid
points: ROWNUM = 1 without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary row
NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery has a NULL
> ALL on an empty subquery is TRUE for every row
MERGE with duplicate source keys fails with ORA-30926
